system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2161-03-17 10:42:00 to 2161-03-22 14:55:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 31-year-old woman with a history of bronchopulmonary dysplasia from prematurity and chronic tracheostomy was admitted for progressive dyspnea and evaluation of her airway. She underwent a rigid bronchoscopy with replacement of her tracheostomy tube to a fenestrated, uncuffed Portex tube. Postoperatively, she developed hoarseness and was found to have supraglottic edema and laryngitis, likely fungal (laryngeal thrush), for which she was started on fluconazole. GERD management was intensified with omeprazole. Her voice improved with rest, and she was discharged home on day four with instructions to continue trach care, complete the antifungal course, and follow up as an outpatient. Thoracic surgery recommended further work-up for long-term management.
problems: Other candidiasis of other specified sites
Acute laryngitis without mention of obstruction

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms ___ is a ___ female w/tracheobronchomalacia s/p 
tracheotomy, asthma, GERD, chronic bronchitis, p/w SOB, 
dizziness, and thick green secretions from her trach. 

#Shortness of breath - It was thought that her symptoms were 
caused by inflammation and increased secretions obstructing the 
trach tube in the setting of a treat and resolving respiratory 
infection. CXR was negative for acute disease. Mild gaseous 
distention of the splenic flexure, without evidence for 
obstruction. CBC showed leukocytosis to 13.7, which trended down 
during her course. Her oxygen saturation was 98-100% on room air 
throughout her hospitalization. Her lung exam was notable for 
expiratory wheeze at the beginning but was CTAB for several days 
before discharge. For this problem, she was put on an aggressive 
expectorant regimen including mucomyst nebs and guaifenesin; 
interventional pulmonology performed bronchoscopy and debrided 
trach secretions. During the course of her hospitalization, Ms. 
___ subsequently became tachycardic >140 in the setting of 
receiving both standing and prn albuterol. ECG was normal 
showing sinus tachycardia. Chest CTA was performed and ruled out 
pulmonary emboli, it subsequently also showed ground glass 
changes that were interpreted by the primary team to be 
consistent with resolving pneumonia. Sputum cultures were 
negative for pathogens. On discharge, her SOB was improved, 
leukocytosis normalized, and she was able to maintain an SpO2 of 
98% after ambulation. 

#Dizziness - Patient complained of dizziness throughout her 
admission, She was found to be orthostatic. She was fluid 
resuscitated with IV fluids, and encouraged to take more POs. 
Her dizziness had resolved on discharge. 

#Tracheobronchomalacia - fiberoptic laryngoscopy in ___ 
showed laryngeal stenosis and scarring and suggested that she 
may not have any closure of her vocal cords. Interventional 
pulmonology was asked to assess airway using bronchoscopy. They 
found ""bronchopulmonary dysplasia with chronic tracheostomy tube 
and laryngeal stenosis status post bronchoscopy with patent 
tracheostomy tube and patent distal airways with minimal 
secretions."" They recommended followup with ENT for their 
recommendations for the laryngeal stenosis. An appointment with 
ENT was made on discharge.

#Asthma - asthma exacerbation may have contributed to her airway 
problems at the beginning of her illness but it was felt to be 
well controlled since patient was treated with short-course 40mg 
prednisone and continued on her outpatient asthma regimen. When 
patient became tachycardic, albuterol was replaced by xopenex 
and frequency of treatments were decreased. On discharge, her 
SpO2 was 98% on RA and she did not have expiratory wheezes on 
lung exam.

#GERD - Not an active issue during this admission, but given her 
upper airway malformation, her omeprazole dose was increased to 
20mg BID to decrease her chances of aspiration pneumonia.

showed laryngeal stenosis and scarring and suggested that she 
may not have any closure of her vocal cords. Interventional 
pulmonology was asked to assess airway using bronchoscopy. They 
found ""bronchopulmonary dysplasia with chronic tracheostomy tube 
and laryngeal stenosis status post bronchoscopy with patent 
tracheostomy tube and patent distal airways with minimal 
secretions."" They recommended followup with ENT for their 
recommendations for the laryngeal stenosis. An appointment with 
ENT was made on discharge.

#Asthma - asthma exacerbation may have contributed to her airway 
problems at the beginning of her illness but it was felt to be 
well controlled since patient was treated with short-course 40mg 
prednisone and continued on her outpatient asthma regimen. When 
patient became tachycardic, albuterol was replaced by xopenex 
and frequency of treatments were decreased. On discharge, her 
SpO2 was 98% on RA and she did not have expiratory wheezes on 
lung exam.

#GERD - Not an active issue during this admission, but given her 
upper airway malformation, her omeprazole dose was increased to 
20mg BID to decrease her chances of aspiration pneumonia.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAM:  Chest frontal and lateral views.

CLINICAL INFORMATION:  ___ female with history of shortness of breath.

___ and ___.

FINDINGS:  Frontal and lateral views of the chest were obtained.  Midline
tracheostomy is again seen.  Lung volumes are slightly low.  No focal
consolidation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax is seen.  The cardiac and
mediastinal silhouettes are unremarkable and unchanged.  There is prominence
of air-filled loops of bowel in the upper abdomen, decreased in amount/size
since the prior study of ___, although the complete abdomen was not
evaluated on this study and clinical correlation with further imaging can be
obtained as clinically warranted.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No acute cardiopulmonary process.

2.  Prominent air distended loops of bowel in the upper abdomen, although less
so than on the prior study from ___ the full abdomen is not evaluated on
this study.  Recommend clinical correlation and further imaging as warranted.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH

INDICATION:  Acute onset of shortness of breath after bronchoscopy, potential
aspiration.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  As compared to the previous radiograph, there is no relevant
change.  Persisting distended bowel loops in the upper abdomen that lead to
elevation of the diaphragm.

The lung volumes are small.  Minimal retrocardiac atelectasis.  No evidence of
pneumothorax.  No pulmonary edema.  No pleural effusions.  No focal
parenchymal opacity suggestive of pneumonia.  Unchanged position of the
tracheostomy tube.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with dilated bowel on chest x-ray and nausea.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal radiograph ___.

FINDINGS:  Supine and erect abdomen radiographs were obtained.  The
radiographs demonstrate gaseous distention of the splenic flexure and
transverse colon measuring up to 8.3 cm.  In comparison to the prior study,
this has not significantly changed.  Fecal material is noted within the distal
descending colon and rectum.  There is no significant  small bowel dilatation.
A linear metallic density overlying the abdomen in the midline likely is
external to the patient (at the level of L4-L5).

The osseous structures appear unremarkable.  There is no free air or
pneumatosis.

IMPRESSION:  Mild gaseous distention of the splenic flexure, without evidence
for obstruction.

CTPA INPATIENT

COMPARISON:  ___.

HISTORY:  Bronchopulmonary dysplasia status post tracheotomy with tachycardia
and pleuritic chest pain, evaluate for PE.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axially acquired images through the chest were obtained.  IV
contrast was administered.  Coronal and sagittal reformats were performed.

FINDINGS:  Patient is status post tracheotomy.  Tracheostomy tube terminates
approximately 3.2 cm above the carina.  There are no filling defects within
the main pulmonary arteries or its branches to suggest pulmonary emboli. Again
identified is a ground-glass opacity within the right upper lobe (2, 23).
There has been interval development of extensive hazy linear opacities within
the right upper lobe (2, 35) and right middle lobe (2, 43).  Patchy round
ground-glass opacities within the bilateral lower lungs (2, 41 and 2, 49) is
also identified.  There is no pericardial or pleural effusion.  The airways
are patent to the subsegmental level.  There is no axillary, hilar or
mediastinal lymphadenopathy.  The heart and great vessels are unremarkable.
There is a small hiatal hernia with an air-fluid level identified within the
distal esophagus.  There is a hypodense thyroid nodule in the right lobe of
the thyroid gland (2, 4).

BONE WINDOWS:  There are no suspicious lytic or sclerotic lesions identified.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Diffuse widespread ground-glass opacity and hazy linear opacity in the
right upper lobe, right middle lobe and bilateral lower lobes.  These findings
are concerning for diffuse infectious process.  Differential diagnosis
includes hemorrhage and less likely edema.
2.  Trace right pleural effusion.
3.  No evidence of pulmonary embolus.
4.  Hiatal hernia.
5.  Thyroid nodule.  Dedicated thyroid ultrasound on a nonurgent basis is
recommended.

Findings were discussed with Dr. ___ by telephone at 7:00 p.m.

diagnoses.long_title: Other diseases of trachea and bronchus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having trouble breathing lately. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it feels like I'm breathing through a straw. It's been getting worse over the past two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And have you noticed any changes in your secretions from the trach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they used to be clear and thin, but now they’re thick and green.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be a sign of infection. You mentioned dizziness too—when does that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yesterday, I felt like the room was spinning. I almost fell when I stood up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your blood pressure when you stand to see if it drops. That could explain the dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also get sharp pain on my sides when I take deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called pleuritic chest pain. We’ll get a CT scan to make sure there’s no clot or pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on cipro and prednisone for five days. I don’t feel any better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes with your airway history, secretions build up and block airflow. The meds might not reach deep enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with IV fluids for dehydration and dizziness. We’ll also do a chest CT and consider a bronchoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bronchoscopy? Is that safe with my trach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can go through your trach. It will help us see if there’s a blockage and clean it out if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray didn’t show pneumonia, but your white blood cell count is rising, which suggests infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the X-ray is normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but sometimes infections don’t show up right away. We’re still concerned and want to rule out a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re scheduling your bronchoscopy for today. It should help clear the secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. Afterward, you might feel a little sore, but it’s usually well tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bronchoscopy went well. They found your airway was patent but had some thick secretions. They cleared them out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that was the problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely a big part of it. Your breathing should improve now that the blockage is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel a bit dizzy when I stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure drops when you stand—orthostatic hypotension. We’re giving IV fluids and encouraging you to drink more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan last night. It shows some hazy spots in your lungs, which could be from infection or inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to say for sure. The spots are patchy. But there’s no pulmonary embolus, which is good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is stabilizing with fluids. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on room air and your oxygen is stable. The bronchoscopy helped. We’re continuing with nebulizers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum culture came back—just normal mouth bacteria, no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop cipro. The green secretions were likely from inflammation, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down, which means your body is calming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel less short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re also adjusting your asthma meds. You were getting too much albuterol, which made your heart race.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel my heart racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched to Xopenex, which is gentler. Your heart rate is normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if things stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the spots on my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re likely from the inflammation and resolving now. No need for further action unless symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my throat issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bronchoscopy showed laryngeal stenosis. We’ve scheduled an ENT follow-up to discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my GERD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We increased your omeprazole to twice daily to reduce aspiration risk, given your airway issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready to go home today. Your breathing is stable, dizziness is gone, and labs are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have trouble breathing, fever, or dizziness again, come back. Otherwise, keep up with trach care and see ENT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send all your discharge instructions and meds with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the thyroid nodule from the CT serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and likely not related. But we recommend a thyroid ultrasound as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up on that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Keep up the good work with your breathing treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel so much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful to hear. We’re glad we could help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I travel soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wait a few days. Make sure you’re stable. Bring your nebulizer if you fly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for all the advice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and call anytime if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 31-year-old woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia, chronic tracheostomy, asthma, and GERD was admitted for worsening shortness of breath, thick green tracheal secretions, and dizziness. She had been on ciprofloxacin and prednisone without improvement. Evaluation revealed leukocytosis and orthostatic hypotension. A bronchoscopy cleared obstructive secretions, leading to symptom improvement. A chest CT showed ground-glass opacities concerning for infection, though sputum cultures were negative, suggesting resolving inflammation. Her tachycardia was linked to albuterol use and resolved with medication adjustment. Dizziness resolved with IV fluid rehydration. The omeprazole dose was increased for GERD prophylaxis. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up arranged for laryngeal stenosis and a thyroid nodule noted on imaging.
